title: Haggai 1:12–15
context: Haggai’s first oracle bears fruit. Zerubbabel, Joshua, and “all the remnant of the people” obey the LORD’s voice and fear him (1:12), and Haggai, “the LORD’s messenger”, brings the promise “I am with you” (1:13). The LORD stirs up the spirit of the leaders and the people, and they begin work on the house on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius (1:14–15), a little over three weeks after the first oracle. Some readers and editions attach the date in 1:15, or part of it, to the oracle that begins in 2:1; the WEB places it at the end of chapter 1, and these notes read it there as dating the start of the work. Compare Ezra 5:2, where Zerubbabel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak begin to build with the prophets helping them. Shared ground: both traditions read these verses as showing that the work began with the LORD’s initiative and the people’s real obedience. They differ on how those two relate, which the Philippians 2:13 box treats.

verses.text: Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the LORD their God’s voice, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the LORD their God had sent him; and the people feared the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the LORD their God’s voice”. Arminian readers hear a real and willing response to the prophetic word, and a reverent fear of the LORD that marks true repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see genuine obedience and godly fear, and they note that the people obeyed the words of Haggai “as the LORD their God had sent him”. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of a community receiving the prophet’s word as the LORD’s word and acting on it together.

verses.text: Then Haggai, the LORD’s messenger, spoke the LORD’s message to the people, saying, “I am with you,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Haggai, “the LORD’s messenger”, brings a short word: “I am with you,” says the LORD. Arminian readers hear the LORD’s assurance meeting the people’s turning, so that their obedience is answered by his presence and encouragement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the covenant promise of the LORD’s presence, which is the ground of the people’s courage and work rather than its reward. Shared ground: both traditions read “I am with you” as the heart of the oracle, repeated in 2:4, and as the promise that makes the rebuilding worthwhile.

verses.text: The LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and worked on the house of the LORD of Armies, their God,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel”, of Joshua, and “of all the remnant of the people”. Arminian readers hear divine enabling met by a real response: the LORD awakens and strengthens the people, and they freely come and work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the LORD’s effectual stirring, which produces the people’s willing obedience, much as the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus and of the returning exiles in Ezra 1:1 and 1:5. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the work began with the LORD’s initiative, and that the people really “came and worked on the house”.

verses.text: in the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The date, “in the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king”, marks when the work began. Arminian readers note the people’s prompt response, a little over three weeks after the first oracle of 1:1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the date as recording the LORD’s word bearing fruit in history. Some readers attach this date, or part of it, to the oracle of 2:1. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as dating the start of the rebuilding, and as showing that the people’s obedience came quickly once the LORD had spoken.
